Pointer Events give one input model for touch, pen and mouse swipes and long-press

sources.claim: Incubation (setting a problem aside) improves later insight in lab studies
A sealed, device-only idea log helps people return to ideas fresh
Bach-y-Rita 1969: camera image projected onto the skin of the back (tactile vision substitution)
Meijer 1992: image-to-sound encoding (The vOICe)
Substitution used to anticipate a lead vehicle (preprint pointed to by @seeingwithsound, 2026-09-30)
A closed glyph code (bar, gap, stack) read by sight or tone gives the same sum: agreement, not acuity
Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC): people communicate intent without speech, using gestures, symbols and switch patterns
Morse code: a two-element timing code (short / long) carries meaning by pattern alone
Non-lexical sounds (uh-huh, mm) carry conversational intent without words
A small personal tap vocabulary is faster than typing for a few frequent intents
The Page Visibility API reports when a page is hidden (another tab or app) and visible again
Gloria Mark's studies: average attention on one screen before switching fell to about 47 seconds
Seeing your own unbroken stretches helps you hold longer ones
DeviceOrientation events report device tilt (beta = front-to-back) and iOS requires an explicit permission request
Tilt-to-scroll was studied as a one-handed reading technique on handhelds (Rekimoto 1996, Tilting operations for small screen interfaces)
A gesture that is off by default and shows its own reading is trusted more than an always-on one
Negative mean asynchrony: people tapping along to a metronome tend to tap tens of milliseconds before the beat
Sensorimotor synchronization research reviews (Repp 2005; Repp & Su 2013)
Seeing your own lead/lag after a round makes the next round steadier
Benchmark floor and skill count over 22 hours, read from this repo's git history (tools/bench.best.json, void-live-deploy/skills/index.json)
Pearson correlation measures linear co-movement, not cause
More skills cause a higher benchmark (rather than both following the same agents' rounds)
35 pull requests merged into atomeam/void-loop on 2026-10-03, by branch lane (claude 12, helper 12, grok 10, forethinkers 1)
The breaks listed (key reaching the answer model, a skill collision, append conflicts, stalled runs) and their fixes
More parallel lanes raised output, and checks can absorb the conflict cost
Inverse document frequency (Sparck Jones 1972): a term in few documents carries more information
The 27 agent log lines of 2026-10-03, ranked by their average rare-word weight
The rarest lines of a day are the ones worth a person's attention
Rising final pitch commonly marks questions and continuation; falling pitch marks statements and finality (intonation in English)
Autocorrelation estimates the fundamental frequency of a voiced sound (de Cheveigné & Kawahara, YIN)
A one-second hum contour (rising / falling / level) is a usable yes / no / wait signal for a person who would rather not speak or type
Void routes an ask to the first ability in skills/index.json whose match() takes it; abilities list nearMisses they must refuse (tools/skills-check.mjs)
Showing people why a system made a decision (explanation interfaces) helps them predict and correct it
Seeing who would answer before asking turns would-be misses into asks people rephrase, so fewer reach the miss board
The Brier score, the mean squared gap between a stated probability and what happened, measures forecast quality; always saying 50% scores 0.25
People who keep score of their probabilistic forecasts become better calibrated over time (Good Judgment Project)
Scoring your own hunches tells you which of your weak signals are worth acting on
Incubation (setting an unsolved problem aside) improves problem solving on average; a meta-analysis of 117 studies found a reliable but modest effect
Sleep between attempts more than doubled the rate of discovering a hidden shortcut in a number task
Writing a stuck problem down at night and revisiting it the next day helps this person, measured by their own hit rate
The psychomotor vigilance task (reacting to a counter shown at random 2-10 s intervals) is a standard, practice-resistant measure of sustained attention
Lapses (reactions of 500 ms or more) on the vigilance task rise steadily with chronic sleep restriction, even when people rate themselves as only slightly sleepy
A short 2-minute home version, logged by time of day, shows when this person is sharpest

Duration judgments differ by paradigm: when people know in advance they will judge time (prospective) their estimates behave differently from when they are asked only afterwards (retrospective), and mental load shifts the two in opposite directions (meta-analysis)
Time that was full of events tends to be remembered as longer, while it often feels shorter while it is happening (the holiday paradox)
When this person knows in advance they will be asked (they mark the start), their duration estimates are biased in a steady direction that depends on whether they were busy or idle
A camera image turned into sound (left to right in time, height as pitch, brightness as loudness) can convey pictures to the ear; this is the design of The vOICe
Blind people trained with a tactile vision-substitution system learned to recognise objects and their layout through touch on the skin
With practice, this person can tell simple shapes apart by sound alone, measured as a hit rate above the 1-in-4 chance level
People using decision aids tend to accept automated suggestions without enough checking (automation bias), including wrong ones, across fields such as aviation and medicine
In clinical decision support, automation bias raised errors when advice was wrong; committing to one's own judgment before seeing the advice is among the suggested mitigations
This person catches more wrong suggestions when they answer before seeing the suggestion than when they see it first
A simple template matcher (resample, rotate, scale, compare) recognizes single-stroke gestures with about 97% accuracy from one example per shape, and 99% with three or more
Gesture-only interfaces hurt usability when gestures are invisible and undiscoverable and give no feedback; an equivalent visible control and clear feedback are recommended
This person's own strokes are read right at least 90% of the time after 20 tries, so drawing could stand in for these four buttons for them
People neglect base rates when judging how likely something is from a specific description (representativeness)
In a large geopolitical forecasting tournament, brief training in probabilistic reasoning (including starting from base rates) made forecasts more accurate
For this person, starting from a base rate and weighing each signal explicitly gives better-scored chances than their gut, over 15 or more resolved hunches
An undemanding task during an incubation break led to more new ideas on a repeated unusual-uses problem than a demanding task, rest, or no break
Incubation effects vary with the kind of problem and what fills the break; a meta-analysis of 117 studies found the effect is larger for divergent (many-answer) problems
For this person, an easy task in the break gives more new ideas than a hard task or rest, measured by their own rounds
Of the UAP reports US officials could resolve, most were ordinary objects such as balloons, birds, drones, aircraft and satellites
Low-orbit satellites, including Starlink, are visible when the observer's sky is dark but the satellite is still sunlit, which concentrates sightings in the hours around dusk and dawn
Checking a personal sighting against the sun's position and a short list of common explanations resolves most of what a person logs
When two targets appear in a rapid stream, the second is often missed if it comes about 200-500 ms after the first, and caught at shorter or longer gaps (the attentional blink)
The blink has been repeated widely and varies between people; second-target accuracy is usually measured only on trials where the first target was reported
A person's own blink can be seen with a few dozen home trials at a handful of gaps, though browser frame timing makes it rougher than a lab's
Blind people trained with a tactile vision substitution system learned to recognise objects and their positions through touch
The vOICe maps image height to pitch and left-right position to time and stereo, and users can learn to read images from sound
A person's miss distance on this two-cue sound task (pitch for height, stereo for side) shrinks over a few dozen trials at home
Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d') from response bias (criterion) in yes/no detection, so a listener who says yes more often is not scored as hearing better
The log-linear correction (add 0.5 to counts, 1 to totals) keeps hit and false-alarm rates of 0 or 1 usable and biases d' less than other fixes
A 2-down 1-up staircase settles near the level where about 71% of signals are detected
A person's own d' for a faint tone in hiss, measured at home with ordinary headphones over about 30 trials, is stable enough to compare day to day
People judging correlation from scatterplots tend to underestimate moderate correlations, and judgments improve toward r = 1
Perceived correlation in scatterplots follows a consistent law across observers, with the largest underestimation at middle values
A person's own middle-band underestimate can be seen in about twenty guesses on a phone screen
People match a made-up word like 'maluma' to a rounded shape and 'takete' to a jagged one far more often than chance
The bouba-kiki match holds across speakers of 25 languages and 10 writing systems, though more weakly in some
Voiceless stops and front vowels lean 'sharp', and sonorants with back rounded vowels lean 'round'
A person's own match rate with randomly built words and randomly drawn shapes, over a few dozen rounds, is clearly above 50%
With a large enough number of chances, any outrageous thing is likely to happen (the law of truly large numbers); many striking coincidences have ordinary explanations
The chance of at least one event in n independent tries, each with chance p, is 1 - (1 - p)^n
Seeing their own chance-only count lowers how much weight people give a single striking coincidence
When people cause a tone by a voluntary key press, the felt gap between press and tone is shorter than when the same events are not self-caused (intentional binding)
Intentional binding is widely used as an implicit measure of the sense of agency, though what it measures is debated
A browser version with a machine-initiated press as the comparison shows the same direction of effect in about 20 trials per condition

When people reproduce time intervals drawn from a range, their reproductions are pulled toward the middle of that range: short intervals are overestimated and long ones underestimated (central tendency, Vierordt's law)
The variability of timed responses grows roughly in proportion to the interval being timed (the scalar property)
Seeing their own slope below 1 helps people notice that their sense of duration is pulled toward recent experience
Flying-bomb hits on south London, believed to be aimed at particular districts, fitted a random (Poisson) distribution
People see streaks and clusters in random sequences and read them as meaningful (the clustering illusion)
Comparing a personal log of odd events against same-size random timelines changes how much people read into a run of events
The time to move to a target grows linearly with the index of difficulty, log2 of distance over width (Fitts's law)
The Shannon form log2(D/W + 1) fits pointing data well and gives throughput in bits per second
Seeing their own time and miss rate by target size changes how people size confirm and destructive buttons
Setting a problem aside for a while (an incubation period) improves later solving on average, with larger effects for creative, divergent problems
Three-word remote-associate puzzles measure finding a word that links distant ideas
Comparing their own solve rates after an immediate return and after a break changes when people choose to step away from a hard problem
About 80% of misspellings are a single insertion, deletion, substitution or transposition of adjacent letters
Allowing one edit when matching recovers most misspelled queries; the optimal string alignment distance counts an adjacent swap as one edit
Seeing which kinds of slips they make under time pressure changes how people judge a tool that misses their typos
Search for a target defined by one feature (colour alone) is about as fast whatever the number of items; search for a conjunction of features slows with each item added
Search slopes form a continuum rather than two clean classes; feature searches cluster near 0 ms per item and conjunction searches higher
Measuring their own cost per item changes how people judge cluttered screens and alerts
Tapping in time with an auditory metronome is more stable than with a visual (flashing) one; asynchrony variability to flashes is roughly two to three times larger
People tend to tap slightly before an auditory beat (negative mean asynchrony)
Seeing their own ear-versus-eye timing changes how people judge visual-only cues as stand-ins for sound
An unexpected (oddball) item in a run of repeated items is judged to last longer than a repeated item of the same physical length
Repeated, predictable items seem shorter, and the size of the effect tracks how predictable the item is (repetition suppression as one proposed cause)
A personal oddball expansion measured on a phone or laptop screen, with frame-rounded lengths, is stable enough across sessions to compare one person over time
Flexible analysis (testing several outcomes and reporting the one that worked) raises the false-positive rate far above the nominal 5%
With k independent tests at level alpha, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - (1 - alpha)^k, and testing each at alpha / k (Bonferroni) holds it at or below alpha
Watching false findings appear in made-up noise makes people slower to accept a single weak signal in their own logs
People revising an estimate after advice move on average only about 20-30% of the way toward the adviser (egocentric discounting), even when the adviser is about as accurate as they are
Averaging one's own estimate with another person's is usually more accurate than choosing either, because their errors partly cancel
Seeing their own weight of advice next to the averaging result makes people lean more on a machine helper of known accuracy
People remember interrupted tasks better than finished ones (the Zeigarnik effect; recall ratio about 1.9 in the original study)
Replications are mixed: a 2023 meta-analysis found no reliable memory advantage for unfinished tasks, though a tendency to return to them held up better
sources.source: Ghibellini and Meier (2023), The hypothesis of the Zeigarnik effect revisited: a meta-analysis, Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

sources.claim: Logging which of one's own stuck problems stay on the mind helps decide which to leave unfinished on purpose before a break
When a smaller group and rarer behaviours share the same proportion, people still judge the smaller group as more linked with the rare (undesirable) behaviours
A meta-analysis finds the distinctiveness-based illusory correlation reliable across studies, with moderate size
This page's one-person version shows the same lean in an individual over repeated runs
In rapid serial visual presentation, a second target 200-500 ms after a correctly reported first target is often missed (the attentional blink), while one right after it (lag 1) is spared
Reviews find the attentional blink robust across many tasks and stimuli, with large individual differences
This page's one-person version shows the dip at 200-300 ms in an individual over about 40 rounds
Classifying a visual target as high or low is faster when an irrelevant tone's pitch matches its position (high tone with high target)
Pitch-elevation is among the most robust crossmodal correspondences across studies and populations
This page's one-person version shows a positive matched-mismatched gap with an interval above 0 after about 60 trials
A filled interval (a continuous tone) is judged longer than an equal empty interval marked only by its start and end
The filled-duration illusion appears across duration ranges and is explained by a faster internal clock during filled intervals
This page's one-person version shows the filled one picked above 50% on equal rounds after about 30 of them
Extreme measurements tend to be followed by ones closer to the average when chance contributes to the measure (regression toward the mean)
Regression to the mean is a common source of misjudged effects in repeated measurements and before-after comparisons, and can be handled with a control group or adjustment
This page's simulation shows the top tenth keeping about as much of its lead as the skill share
People who see an algorithm err become less likely to use it than a human forecaster who errs, even when the algorithm is more accurate (algorithm aversion)
Before seeing it fail, people often weight algorithmic advice more than human advice (algorithm appreciation)
This page's one-person version shows a higher leave rate after the helper loses a round than after it wins, about 30 rounds in
Misleading cues planted beside remote-associate puzzles lowered first-try solving, and an incubation interval helped mostly by letting the fixation fade
An incubation break improved remote-associate solving only for people who had first been given misleading cues
Logging one's own second-try solves after a wrong lead, with and without a break, shows whether stepping away helps this person mainly when they are stuck on a wrong idea
Windows counts two clicks as a double click when the second comes within the double-click time, 500 ms by default
Mobile browsers waited about 300 ms after a tap to see whether a second tap (double-tap to zoom) followed
A double-tap window fitted to one person's own double taps and separate tap pairs makes fewer errors for them than a fixed 300 or 500 ms window
Naming the ink colour of a colour word is slower when the word names a different colour (the Stroop effect)
Half a century of Stroop studies finds the interference robust across many variations of the task
A person's own Stroop cost, logged per sitting with the hour of day, is higher at their tired times and can tell them when focused work will cost more
People tap in time with an auditory beat far more steadily than with a visual flash, and when both are given together the auditory beat mostly governs the timing
Decades of tapping studies show auditory metronomes give smaller and steadier asynchronies than visual ones
A person's own tapping spread with sound, flash and both shows which sense carries timing best for them, a guide to which sense a substitution device should use for timing

When people reproduce intervals drawn from a range, short ones come out too long and long ones too short (central tendency, Vierordt's law), and the pull grows with timing uncertainty as a Bayesian observer would predict
Vierordt's 1868 study of the time sense first reported that short durations are overestimated and long ones underestimated around an indifference point
A person's own reproduction slope and indifference point, fitted from their tries, show how strongly their timing leans on what is usual
People judging how likely something is from a sign tend to neglect how rare it was to begin with (base-rate neglect)
Stating the same information as natural frequencies (counts out of a whole) instead of percentages makes far more people reason correctly about it
Seeing each of one's own percentage guesses redrawn as counts out of 1,000 shrinks one's base-rate error over rounds
People monitoring an automated system detected far fewer of its failures when its reliability stayed constant than when it varied over time (automation-induced complacency)
Complacency and automation bias appear when attention is spread over several tasks and are not limited to novices
A person's own catch rate for an autopilot's misses is lower in steady blocks than in changing blocks, and seeing that gap changes how closely they watch
People read goals and intentions into simple geometric shapes moving on a screen
Detecting a chase among moving dots falls steeply as the chaser's heading is allowed to wander further off the direct line (chasing subtlety), approaching chance near 90 degrees
A person's own d' for spotting a chase drops with chasing subtlety in the same way, measured on this page
In a threshold system, a moderate amount of added noise can make a sub-threshold signal more detectable than either no noise or a lot of noise (stochastic resonance)
People viewing sub-threshold images rendered through a noisy threshold perceive them best at an intermediate noise level
A person's own accuracy at telling an upright from a flat faint bar peaks at a middle noise level on this page
Restricting a sample to a narrow range of one variable lowers the observed correlation, by an amount Thorndike's case II formula predicts from the spread kept
Validity coefficients computed among already-selected people (admitted, hired) understate the predictor's correlation in the full applicant pool
People looking at a shaded band of a scatter plot under-predict how much weaker its correlation is, measured on this page
In a self-exciting point process each event raises the chance of more soon after, so events cluster beyond what independent random arrivals give
For events arriving independently at random, daily counts have variance about equal to their mean (index of dispersion near 1), testable with a chi-square statistic
A person's own log of odd moments bunches more than chance, as attention after one makes the next more noticeable, measured on this page
The probability that the next observation is of a species not yet seen is estimated by the share of species seen exactly once (Good-Turing)
The total number of classes in a population, seen or not, can be estimated from the counts of classes seen once and twice (Chao1)
Applied to a miss board, the share of kinds seen once predicts the share of next week's misses that are new kinds
One flash paired with two beeps is often seen as two flashes (the sound-induced flash illusion)
People weigh each sense by how reliable it is when the senses disagree
A short self-run test in a browser, with uncontrolled timing and speakers, still shows the pull for a given person
A cue that points to where a target will appear speeds the response, and a misleading cue slows it (spatial cueing)
Detection of a simple signal is faster at a location attention was directed to in advance, and slower at an unexpected one
A person's own cost of a misleading pointer, logged per sitting with the hour of day, varies with their time of day in a way they could use
Variability in timing grows in proportion to the interval timed (the scalar property of interval timing)
Across many studies the scalar property holds roughly for intervals from about a few hundred milliseconds to seconds, with departures at the extremes
A person's own spread share (sd/mean) and how level it stays across lengths is steady enough from sitting to sitting to be a personal timing signature
Listeners judge a speaker who answers after a longer pause or a filler as less likely to know the answer (the feeling of another's knowing)
Speakers use 'uh' and 'um' to signal a coming delay, 'um' a longer one
One person's weights on pause length and on 'um' when judging another's knowing are steady across sittings and differ between people
A cumulative sum of deviations from a target, less an allowance, detects a small sustained shift in a process mean faster than looking at single readings (Page's CUSUM)
CUSUM with an allowance of half a standard deviation and a decision interval of about five standard deviations is a common choice for detecting a one-sd shift
Run on a person's own daily numbers, CUSUM flags a lasting change before the person would have noticed it

People responding to one stimulus type beside a partner who responds to the other show a spatial compatibility effect that largely disappears when they do the same single-key task alone (the joint Simon effect)
A visible machine partner on screen draws a joint-Simon cost from a person, and that cost is steady enough per person to read their sense of acting with a machine
An association that holds within every subgroup can vanish or reverse when the subgroups are pooled (Simpson's paradox)
Berkeley's 1973 graduate admissions looked biased against women when pooled, while most departments, taken one by one, showed no such bias
Seeing a pooled number of one's own split out by group changes how a person reads it
The time to move to a target grows linearly with log2(distance / width + 1), the index of difficulty (Fitts's law)
Fitts's law fits pointing with mice, styluses and touch well enough to be a standard tool for sizing interface targets
Sizing a button or an opt-in gesture to one person's own fitted line makes it easier for them than a one-size rule
Responses to a central target letter are slowed when the flanking letters call for the other response (the flanker effect)
The flanker cost is smaller on a trial that follows an incongruent trial than on one that follows a congruent trial (conflict adaptation, the Gratton effect)
Part of that sequence effect comes from exact stimulus repeats rather than adaptation to conflict, so the shrink is not pure control
A person's own crowd cost and its shrink after conflict, tracked over sittings at home, are stable enough to notice a change in how focused they are

hypothesis: A 48-row flanker sitting in the browser can measure a person's own crowd cost and whether it shrinks right after a row that fought them, without any server.
behavior: five arrows, answer the middle one; the cost of disagreeing neighbours in ms, split by the row before (the Gratton effect), kept per sitting in this browser only
findings: the after-row split needs both rows correct and leaves about a dozen rows per cell in one sitting, so the draft asks for about six sittings before reading the shrink

failure_modes.what: exact repeats of the same row inflate the after-conflict shrink
failure_modes.evidence: Mayr, Awh and Laurey (2003, https://doi.org/10.1038/nn1051) found the sequence effect largely vanished once exact repeats were removed; this draft does not remove them yet

next_experiments: drop exact stimulus repeats from the after-row split and compare the shrink with and without them
